title: Nearby drivers at scale
description: A ride-hailing service has 500,000 online drivers who each send a location every 5 seconds. Riders need the nearest available drivers within about 3 km in under 100 ms. The team proposes storing locations in the main Postgres database with a PostGIS GiST index and updating the row on every ping. What is the best alternative?

options.text: Keep PostGIS but add read replicas so nearby queries do not hit the primary
options.explanation: Replicas spread reads, but the bottleneck is 100,000 durable index updates per second on one primary, and replicas would lag behind fast-moving drivers.

options.text: Store a geohash per driver and query only the rider's own geohash cell
options.explanation: Querying one cell misses drivers just across a cell boundary; geohash search must include neighbouring cells and filter by distance.

options.text: Use a composite B-tree index on (lat, lng) instead of GiST to make updates cheaper
options.explanation: A composite B-tree narrows only latitude, so a proximity query scans a band around the globe, and the write load problem remains.

options.text: Stream pings into an in-memory geo index sharded by region, keyed by cell with TTL expiry, and search the cell plus expanding rings
options.explanation: About 100,000 updates per second of short-lived data fits in memory per region; TTLs drop offline drivers and ring expansion with exact distance filtering finds the nearest candidates quickly.
